column5: death sought but cannot be found
column6: Under locust torment people seek death and cannot find it; like the fire-dweller of 87:13, torment continues while the normal exit of death is withheld.

column5: corpses, undying worm, unquenched fire
column6: Isaiah calls the rebels corpses, while the worm does not die and the fire is not quenched; that allocation differs from the commentary's conscious fire-inhabitant who is neither dead nor alive.

column5: undying souls in Gehinnom
column6: The Targum turns Isaiah's corpse-and-fire scene into punishment in Gehinnom in which the sinners' souls do not die, an interpretive move that closely approaches the commentary's deathless fire.

column5: eternal punitive death without extinction
column6: Augustine argues that the damned can endure punitive death without being annihilated; this gives a Christian account of the continuing, non-living condition the commentary marks in 87:13.

column5: fire and sulfur torment
column6: The beast-worshiper is tormented with fire and sulfur, a concrete New Testament fire-punishment scene beside the commentary's fire where death does not end suffering.

column5: no rest day or night, smoke forever
column6: The people under judgment have no rest day or night and their torment's smoke rises forever; this specifically parallels the commentary's exclusion of sleep or a recoverable lapse in the fire.

column5: torment day and night forever
column6: The devil, beast, and false prophet are tormented day and night for ever and ever, supplying an explicit Christian image of punitive remaining rather than release through death.

column5: source label م و ت B012; sleep of death
column6: The psalm asks not to sleep the sleep of death; Hebrew מָוֶת is a genuine cognate of the source label م و ت, and the verse supplies the sleep-as-death figure that the commentary says is unavailable in the fire.

column5: sleepers in dust awaken to enduring fates
column6: Those sleeping in dust awaken, some to everlasting life and some to disgrace; it makes the commentary's sleep, life, and lasting afterlife distinctions into two final outcomes rather than the suspended state of 87:13.

column5: sleep and promised awakening
column6: Jesus calls Lazarus asleep and says that he will awaken him, a recoverable sleep-state set against the commentary's insistence that the fire offers neither sleep nor waking.

column5: death when divine breath is withdrawn
column6: When God takes away creatures' breath, they die and return to dust; this concretizes the commentary's source definition of death as strength or life-force withdrawn from a thing.

column5: source label ح ي ي B013; life and good versus death and evil
column6: Moses places life and good over against death and evil; Hebrew חַיִּים is cognate with the source label ح ي ي, and the explicit life/good pairing closely supports the commentary's secondary definition of life as benefit and goodness.

column5: source label ح ي ي B013; desiring life and seeing good
column6: The psalm joins desiring life with loving days in order to see good; its Hebrew life-word is cognate with ح ي ي and gives a precise biblical analogue to the commentary's life/good connection.

column5: future treasure and the life that is truly life
column6: Generous use of wealth lays a foundation for the future so that one may grasp "the life that is truly life"; it is a pointed counterpart to choosing near worldly life over the enduring real life.

column5: perishing food and food enduring to eternal life
column6: Jesus contrasts food that perishes with food that endures to eternal life, directly framing a present material pursuit against an abiding life as the commentary does in 87:16-17.

column5: world passes away, God-doer abides forever
column6: The world and its desire are passing away, while the one who does God's will abides forever; this is a close formulation of transient worldly life against lasting life.

column5: no enduring city here, one to come
column6: Believers have no lasting city here but seek the city to come, making the commentary's near-life and abiding-hereafter contrast spatial and communal.

column5: seen temporary, unseen eternal
column6: The seen is temporary and the unseen eternal; its explicit temporal-eternal contrast supplies the evaluative frame of "better and more enduring" in 87:17.

column5: one hour in this world and one hour in the world to come
column6: Avot says both that repentance and good deeds in this world outweigh all life in the world to come and that one hour of bliss there outweighs all life here; its two-sided valuation complicates a simple worldly-life versus afterlife ranking.

column5: good things in lifetime, anguish after death
column6: Abraham contrasts the rich man's good things in his lifetime with his present anguish and Lazarus's comfort; the story concretely tests the commentary's claim that preferring the near life ends in a radically different final condition.

column5: tyrant's torture and everlasting renewal of life
column6: A tortured brother tells the king that the King of the universe will raise the faithful to an everlasting renewal of life; like the commentary's Pharaoh-and-magicians scene, a ruler's bodily threat is answered by appeal to durable divine life.

column5: resurrection to life denied to the persecutor
column6: The martyr tells the king that he will have no resurrection to life, a direct two-fate response to tyrannical violence that sharpens the commentary's contrast between punishment and the purified person's recompense.

column5: faithful people before a king's fiery threat
column6: The three Judeans tell the king that their God can rescue them from the blazing furnace and from his hand; this supplies a scriptural tyrant, fire, and faithful confession beside Pharaoh's threatened believers.

column5: Egyptian magicians name God's finger while Pharaoh hardens
column6: Moses' Egyptian magicians identify the plague as God's finger, but Pharaoh remains hard; the shared Moses-magicians-Pharaoh scene differs from the commentary's magicians who openly believe and receive Pharaoh's threat.

column5: Jannes and Jambres oppose Moses
column6: The letter names Jannes and Jambres as opponents of Moses and compares false teachers to them; this Christian memory of the magicians reverses the commentary's scene of Pharaoh's magicians becoming faithful.

column5: source label ح ي ي B006; daughters are to be kept alive
column6: Pharaoh orders the midwives to kill a Hebrew son but let a daughter live; it is the biblical Pharaoh setting that makes the commentary's "leave your women alive" formula a concrete survival claim.

column5: source label ح ي ي B006; keep every female alive
column6: Moses asks whether the women have all been kept alive; Hebrew הַחִיִּיתֶם uses the cognate life root and gives a sharply specific biblical use of the source commentary's "leaving women alive" sense.

column5: source label ب ق ي B003; preserve a remnant and keep alive
column6: Joseph says God sent him ahead to preserve a remnant and keep the family alive; this joins remaining after threatened extinction to living, precisely the relation developed under the commentary's remaining/sparing branch.

column5: God kills and makes alive
column6: God declares, "I kill and I make alive"; this is a direct Hebrew Bible formulation for the commentary's claim that Abraham assigns both death and life to the Lord.

column5: God kills, makes alive, lowers and raises
column6: Hannah's hymn says that the Lord kills and makes alive and brings down to Sheol and raises; it gives a fuller scriptural pattern of divine control over the two poles named in the commentary.

column5: Father raises the dead and gives life
column6: As the Father raises the dead and gives life, so the Son gives life to whom he wishes; this is a direct Christian articulation of death and life as divine acts.

column5: Abraham expects God to raise the dead
column6: Hebrews reads Abraham's offering of Isaac through resurrection: he considers God able to raise even from the dead. That interpretation makes the commentary's Abrahamic death-and-life confession into a specific remembered test.

column5: serpent promises no death
column6: The serpent tells the woman that she will not surely die; this is the Torah's direct temptation by a denial of death beside the commentary's satanic offer of a tree of immortality.

column5: tree of life and living forever
column6: God bars the human from eating the tree of life and living forever; its actual tree-and-everlasting-life scene provides the closest biblical counterpart to the commentary's deceptive tree of immortality.

column5: humankind created for incorruption
column6: Wisdom says God created humans for incorruption and made them in the image of divine eternity; it supplies a late Jewish account of true enduring life against the commentary's false promise of permanence.

column5: death enters through the devil's envy
column6: Wisdom attributes death's entrance into the world to the devil's envy, a direct Jewish development of the Adam-and-tempter relation that illuminates the commentary's satanic lure of immortality.

column5: the devil offers earthly kingdoms
column6: The devil offers Jesus all the kingdoms shown to him if Jesus will worship him; this is a Christian temptation scene in which the tempter offers dominion, alongside the commentary's offer of an imperishable kingdom to Adam.

column5: everlasting dominion that will not pass away
column6: The Son of Man receives a dominion that is everlasting and will not pass away; it supplies a divinely granted, genuinely imperishable rule in contrast to the commentary's satanic promise of a kingdom that does not wear out.

column5: water makes everything live where the river goes
column6: Every living creature lives wherever Ezekiel's eschatological river goes; this is a close prophetic counterpart to the commentary's paradise water that vivifies whatever it reaches.

column5: river of water of life in the final paradise
column6: John's final city contains a river of the water of life flowing from God's throne, a directly corresponding paradise-water image for the commentary's life-giving water.

column5: tree of life and leaves for healing
column6: Beside the river stands the tree of life whose leaves heal the nations; it brings the commentary's life-water and immortality-tree images together in the final garden.

column5: living water wells up to eternal life
column6: Jesus promises water that becomes a spring welling up to eternal life, making life-giving water an interior and enduring reality rather than merely a garden image.

column5: the dead live, dust-dwellers awake
column6: Isaiah calls the dead to live and the dust-dwellers to awake and sing; this eschatological reversal is the positive opposite of the commentary's fire where neither death concludes nor life begins.

column5: one who dies will live
column6: Jesus identifies himself as resurrection and life and promises life to the believer who dies; it supplies a concise Christian answer to the commentary's contrast between ordinary death and true enduring life.

column5: eternal punishment and eternal life
column6: The final judgment divides people between eternal punishment and eternal life; its paired lasting destinies are a direct comparison for the commentary's fire and enduring afterlife.

column5: fading grass and the word standing forever
column6: Grass withers and the flower fades, but God's word stands forever; this concrete transient/enduring contrast supports the commentary's evaluation of the near life against what remains.

column5: people longing for death do not find it
column6: Job describes sufferers who long for death but cannot find it; although it is not a fire judgment, it gives a specific suffering-and-unavailable-death analogue to the commentary's secondary Qur'anic comparison.

column5: profit from the world and forfeiting one's life
column6: Jesus asks what profit there is in gaining the whole world while forfeiting one's life; the profit/life juxtaposition closely engages the commentary's claim that life includes benefit and its warning about choosing the worldly life.

column5: temporary enjoyment versus suffering with God's people
column6: Moses chooses mistreatment with God's people over the temporary enjoyment of sin, a Pharaoh-linked Christian reading of a choice between passing advantage and a more durable divine horizon.

column5: water requested in flame
column6: The rich man in flame asks for a drop of water to cool his tongue; it sets a denied water-image inside punitive fire against the commentary's paradise water that confers life.

column5: ordinary Gehinnom judgment limited to twelve months
column6: Mishnah Eduyot limits the ordinary judgment of the wicked in Gehinnom to twelve months; that rabbinic duration qualifies the commentary's image of remaining in fire without death.

column5: righteous called living in death, wicked dead in life
column6: The rabbinic maxim calls the righteous living even in death and the wicked dead even while alive; it makes life and death moral-spiritual categories, a useful interpretive comparison for the commentary's non-biological definition of life as good and benefit.

column5: death will be no more
column6: In the final renewed creation death is no more; this is the eschatological antithesis to the commentary's punitive place where death is indefinitely withheld.

column5: life as a vapor that appears briefly
column6: James calls present life a vapor appearing for a little while and vanishing, a concrete Christian account of the brevity implied by the commentary's name for the near life.

column5: treasure in heaven not destroyed
column6: Jesus directs disciples to treasure in heaven where decay and theft do not destroy; it translates the commentary's contrast between perishable present possession and what remains into a practice of investment.

column5: eternal destruction as punishment
column6: The disobedient suffer "eternal destruction" away from the Lord; the wording gives a Christian punitive alternative to 87:13's unusual condition in which the condemned do not die, while leaving the meaning of destruction to be read in its own context.

column5: reputation of life but actual death
column6: The Sardis church has a name of being alive but is dead; this non-biological use of life and death concretely parallels the commentary's definition of life by active goodness rather than mere survival.

column5: not leaving any breathing thing alive
column6: The ban commands that no breathing thing be left alive, using survival as the opposite of total extirpation; this gives a concrete Hebrew Bible counterpart to the commentary's remaining/sparing sense of life.

column5: believers who sleep and hope beyond grief
column6: Paul calls the deceased "those who sleep" and contrasts believers' grief with those without hope; this Christian death-as-sleep idiom supplies the recoverable horizon that the commentary denies to the fire-dweller.

column5: entering life versus Gehenna's unquenchable fire
column6: Jesus contrasts entering life, even maimed, with being cast into Gehenna's unquenchable fire; it directly joins the commentary's two outcomes of real life and fire rather than merely naming punishment.

column5: worm does not die and fire is not quenched
column6: Mark reapplies the Isaiah image within Jesus' Gehenna teaching: the worm does not die and the fire is not quenched. It supplies a Christian continuation of the deathless, unextinguished fire imagery, while the undying subject remains the worm rather than the punished person.

column5: body and soul destroyed in Gehenna
column6: Jesus distinguishes human killing of the body from God's ability to destroy both body and soul in Gehenna; this provides a concrete Christian counter-formula to the commentary's fire in which the condemned do not die.

column5: lake of fire identified as the second death
column6: The lake burning with fire and sulfur is called the second death. The identification gives the Christian fire a death-name, in pointed contrast to 87:13's non-dying condition.

column5: death as sleep without awakening
column6: A human being lies down and does not rise, not waking or being roused from sleep until the heavens are no more; Job supplies the unrecovered sleep/death image whose absence is developed in the commentary.

column5: death swallowed forever and tears wiped away
column6: God swallows up death forever and wipes tears from faces; this is a prophetic final reversal of the commentary's place where death does not provide release and true life is absent.

column5: torture refused for a better resurrection
column6: Some are tortured and refuse release in order to obtain a better resurrection; this is a direct martyr-and-tyrant counterpart to the commentary's believing magicians facing Pharaoh's violence for a more lasting outcome.

column5: departure to be with Christ is far better
column6: Paul calls departing to be with Christ "far better," an unusually explicit Christian comparative for the commentary's assertion that the afterlife is better than the near life.

column5: earthly tent and eternal heavenly house
column6: The earthly tent is contrasted with an eternal house in the heavens not made by hands; the image maps present bodily life and a durable future dwelling onto the commentary's transient/enduring division.

column5: mortality swallowed up by life
column6: Paul says that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life, a concise Christian expression of life overcoming mortality that illuminates the commentary's definition of true life as permanence.

column5: perishable body raised imperishable
column6: Resurrection is sown perishable and raised imperishable; it gives a bodily account of the enduring life set over against death in the commentary.

column5: passing from death into life
column6: The believer has passed from death into life and does not come into judgment, a compact Johannine two-destiny formulation beside 87:13's denied life in punishment.

column5: tree of life in God's paradise
column6: The conqueror is granted food from the tree of life in God's paradise; this is a final Christian counterpart to the commentary's tree of immortality and its distinction between deceptive and true permanence.

column5: waters of life and tears removed
column6: The Lamb guides the redeemed to springs of waters of life and God wipes every tear; it combines the commentary's paradise water that gives life with an eschatological relief opposite fire-torment.

column5: water of life given freely to the thirsty
column6: God gives the thirsty person water from the spring of life without payment; it is a direct final-life-water analogue to the commentary's revivifying water in paradise.

column5: fountain of life with God
column6: The psalm calls God's presence the fountain of life; it offers a Hebrew poetic precursor for the commentary's link between life, a divine source, and life-giving water.

column5: living waters flow in every season
column6: Living waters flow from Jerusalem both in summer and winter, an eschatological water image whose ongoing flow is a close counterpart to the commentary's paradise water and abiding life.

column5: God's Spirit put within the dead so they live
column6: God promises to put his spirit within the restored people so that they live; this specifies divine reanimation by a life-giving force, the positive opposite of the fire's absence of life.

column5: hope full of immortality despite apparent punishment
column6: Though the righteous seem punished in human sight, their hope is full of immortality; this late Jewish reversal of apparent death and suffering closely complements the commentary's true, enduring life.

column5: furnace of Gehenna opposite paradise of delight
column6: 4 Ezra displays the furnace of Gehenna opposite the place of rest and paradise of delight, a Jewish apocalyptic pairing that makes the commentary's fire and true-life alternatives into adjacent final scenes.

column5: this world as corridor before the world to come
column6: Avot calls this world a corridor before the world to come and urges preparation here; its spatial-temporal image closely frames the commentary's near worldly life as preparatory rather than abiding.

column5: world to come without bodily needs, righteous enjoy divine splendor
column6: The rabbinic description removes eating, drinking, and other bodily satisfactions from the world to come while the righteous enjoy divine splendor; it offers a specific Jewish construal of the commentary's true life as more than ordinary worldly vitality.

column5: eternal fire that punishes without consuming
column6: Tertullian's final-judgment account treats eternal fire as ongoing punishment rather than a fire that simply consumes its victims, a patristic counterpart to the commentary's persistent fire; the precise translation should be verified.

column5: a fixed chasm prevents passage
column6: The great chasm between the tormented rich man and Lazarus is fixed so that no one can cross; this continuation of the water-and-fire scene adds the commentary's concern with remaining in a condition without an exit.

column5: Egyptian riches set against a future reward
column6: Moses considers reproach greater wealth than Egypt's treasures because he looks to the reward; it separately supplies the Egypt-specific valuation of durable reward over near advantage developed in 87:16-17.

column5: sin's wage death, God's gift eternal life
column6: Paul pairs sin's wage of death with God's gift of eternal life, a moral and eschatological life/death contrast that extends the commentary's link between life, goodness, and final outcome.

column5: sowing to flesh yields corruption, Spirit yields eternal life
column6: Sowing to the flesh reaps corruption while sowing to the Spirit reaps eternal life; its present choice and later harvest closely match the commentary's worldly preference and enduring consequence.

column5: earthly-minded people have destruction as their end
column6: Those whose minds are set on earthly things have destruction as their end; this makes the commentary's choice of near life into a concrete moral orientation and eschatological consequence.

column5: heavenly citizenship
column6: Believers' citizenship is in heaven, giving the alternative to the preceding earthly-minded end a communal home that resonates with the commentary's enduring hereafter.

column5: the dead know nothing and have no further reward
column6: Qohelet says the dead know nothing and no longer have reward; within its under-the-sun argument, this is a sharp Hebrew Bible counterpoint to the commentary's afterlife as the locus of true life.

column5: the living thank God
column6: Hezekiah says that the living, the living give thanks to God; it makes active grateful goodness a mark of life, supporting the commentary's claim that bare survival without benefit or good is not life in the full sense.

column5: riches do not profit on the day of wrath
column6: Riches do not profit on the day of wrath, while righteousness delivers from death; the proverb joins the commentary's benefit-language to a final reckoning that defeats merely worldly acquisition.

column5: righteous path is life and has no death
column6: The path of righteousness is life and its way has no death; this ethical use of life gives a precise Hebrew counterpart to the commentary's definition of life through good.

column5: fear of God as a fountain of life
column6: The fear of the Lord is a fountain of life that turns one from death's snares; it gives an ethical-metaphorical use of life-water, distinct from the commentary's paradise-water image.

column5: shares and exclusions in the world to come
column6: The mishnah grants all Israel a share in the world to come while listing exclusions; it gives a Jewish interpretive map of who receives enduring future life, relevant to the commentary's final division without claiming the same criteria.

column5: Sheol and death in a disputed redemption formula
column6: Hosea speaks of ransoming from Sheol and redeeming from death, but the grammar and immediate judgment context make its force disputed; its later life-over-death reception remains a cautious counterpart to the commentary's final death/life contrast.
